I used Tumblr for a few years after its inception.

In the early years it attracted a creative crowd. It was the trendy platform, compared to Blogspot, which was boring; LiveJournal, which was dying; WordPress, which was too tech-y (at the time I don’t think WordPress.com existed, only the self-hosted software). Many artists, musicians, writers were moving their blogs to Tumblr.

It also had a local focus. There were meetups organised, and these were supported by Tumblr semi-officially. I attended two in my city (far away from the US; they were really pushing local groups around the world); Tumblr offices actually sent us stickers and other merch.

I don’t know where the current groups that are associated with Tumblr came from. I never saw the kind of content that is referred to these days, because you only saw content from people that you followed. In that sense it is no different from other social media platforms like Twitter or Facebook. I met some genuinely interesting people in my region, again mostly the creative type. A few artists, musicians. Couple of them are now my good friends IRL, although none of us use Tumblr any more. I think we outgrew blogging in general.

But anyway, my point is Tumblr is just a platform, and like any platform, there are crazies. There are also sane people who use Tumblr, but you won’t hear about them on other platforms because that’s not interesting.
